passage: By 6 a.m. Jaya was on the terrace of her Hyderabad hostel with her guitar, playing the same four bars over and over until they sounded right. By 9 a.m. she was in the electronics lab, yawning over a circuit board. She had chosen engineering with her eyes open: her father's shop had nearly closed twice, and she wanted a job that paid on time. She didn't regret it, exactly. Her friend Gautam noticed the difference, though. "In lab you look like you're waiting for a bus," he said. "On the terrace you look like you forgot the time." Jaya laughed, but it stung a little. That evening she did her circuit homework properly, then played for an hour, and didn't feel guilty about either.

qa.q: Why had Jaya chosen engineering?
qa.a: Her father's shop had nearly closed twice, and she wanted a job that paid on time.

qa.q: Why might Gautam's remark sting Jaya a little?
qa.a: It named a split she already feels: she values engineering's security, but her energy lights up for music, and both reasons matter to her.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make that evening, and why might it help?
qa.a: She did her circuit homework properly and then played for an hour, honouring both sets of reasons instead of forcing herself to pick one.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Jaya in the lab and on the terrace?
qa.a: Gautam sees two different energies: someone waiting for a bus in the lab, and someone who forgets the time with the guitar.

grounding: A student chose engineering for security while music pulls at her, and the difference shows in her energy.

'You're playing again at midnight?' Nandini Apa stood in the doorway in her nightclothes.
Farida lowered the harmonium lid. 'Just ten minutes. I finished the thermodynamics sheet first.'
'Ammi says you're wasting engineering fees.'
'I'm not wasting anything. I chose engineering, Apa. I want a salary. I never want to borrow the way Abbu did.' Farida rubbed her eyes. 'But when I sing, it's the only time I'm not counting.'
'Counting what?'
'Marks. Money. Years.' She looked at the harmonium. 'In class I do my best, but it's like pushing a cart. Here, the cart pushes me.'
Nandini came in and sat on the bed. 'So do both. Just don't sing at midnight before a lab exam, okay?'
Farida smiled for the first time that evening. 'Okay.'

passage: I'm Karthik, and I'm in the third year of civil engineering. I picked it for two reasons: my uncle said the jobs are steady, and I liked the idea of never worrying about rent. Faculty mentor's note, second-year electronics. Wasim.
Suraj came for his mid-semester review today. Marks fine, attendance fine, but he says he 'drags himself' to lab. When I asked why electronics, he was honest: 'My father's shop closed two years ago. I want a job that doesn't disappear.' That's a real reason, and I told him so.
Then I mentioned I'd heard him on tabla at the cultural night. His whole face changed. He talked for ten minutes about a rhythm cycle he's composing, hands tapping the desk.
He isn't choosing wrongly; he's pulled two ways, and the pull is draining him.
Next steps: I suggested the audio signal processing elective next term and told him about the college's recording room. We'll meet again after exams to see where his energy goes.

qa.q: What instrument did Wasim hear Suraj play at the cultural night?
qa.a: The tabla.

qa.q: Why did Suraj choose electronics, and what does his face at the mention of tabla suggest?
qa.a: Suraj wants a secure job after his father's shop closed, a real need; but his face changing and his hands tapping suggest music is what truly excites him.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices respects both of Suraj's motives, and why?
qa.a: Suggesting the audio signal processing elective and the recording room; it keeps the secure path while giving music a place, which may bring back some energy.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father see this tension if he knew about it?
qa.a: His father might be relieved that Suraj chose security after the shop closed, yet sad to learn that his son drags himself to lab while lighting up for music.

grounding: A mentor notes a student who chose electronics for job security while drawn to music, with both motives real and the tension draining his energy.

passage:
Thursday
Surveying practical in the sun from nine to one. I measured the wrong baseline twice and Rubina had to redo it. My head was full of the tune I started on Monday.
Here's the thing I don't say out loud: I'm not sorry I took civil. Abbu's salary won't stretch forever, the placement numbers are good, and I like knowing I'll be able to pay Ammi's rent one day. That's real. That matters to me.
But tonight I finished the second verse on Rubina's old keyboard, and it felt as if the whole day had been waiting for that one hour.
Rubina said, 'Sehar, you're two different people. One of them is very sleepy.'
She's right. I don't know how to be both yet. Maybe I don't have to pick. Maybe I just have to stop pretending one of them doesn't exist.

qa.q: What did Sehar finish on Rubina's old keyboard?
qa.a: The second verse of the tune started on Monday.

qa.q: Why does Sehar say 'I'm not sorry I took civil' while dreaming of music?
qa.a: Sehar genuinely values security, helping Abbu and Ammi and getting a good placement; that and the love of songwriting are both real, which is why the day feels split.

qa.q: What choice is Sehar starting to make at the end, and why might it help?
qa.a: To stop pretending the music side doesn't exist instead of picking one; admitting both motives could let Sehar plan time for music and bring more energy to civil too.

qa.q: How does Rubina see Sehar's two sides?
qa.a: Rubina sees 'two different people', a sleepy one in surveying and a lively one at the keyboard, and has had to cover the mistakes; she notices the tension clearly.

passage: In Satara, Aditi cycled every morning to the government engineering college, where her seat in civil engineering had made her father stand a little taller at the milk dairy. A government job someday, a pension, a house with a proper roof: she wanted those things too, honestly. But on Thursday evenings, in the temple courtyard, she sang abhangs with the village women, and her voice filled the whole square. Her cousin Eshaan, home from Pune, heard her one Thursday. 'You don't sound like that about bridges,' he said. Aditi laughed, then stopped. In class she took neat notes and forgot them by evening. At the temple she remembered every line after one hearing. 'I like bridges,' she said slowly. 'I love this.' Eshaan waited. 'Both are true,' she said. 'I just don't know how much of me each one gets.'

qa.q: What did Aditi sing on Thursday evenings?
qa.a: She sang abhangs with the village women.

qa.q: What does Aditi mean by 'I don't know how much of me each one gets'?
qa.a: She feels torn between real reasons for engineering, security and her father's pride, and a deep love of singing, and senses the pull is dividing her energy.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to live with both motives?
qa.a: She could keep engineering for security while protecting regular time for singing, and look for parts of her course that connect to what she enjoys.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Aditi's two sides?
qa.a: Eshaan notices she comes alive singing in a way she doesn't about bridges, and gives her space to say it.

passage: In Kraków, Marek's computer science lectures started at eight, and he made them every day. He had chosen the course for good reasons: his parents had struggled after the factory closed, and programmers were hired everywhere. He wanted that security, badly. But in the evenings he played violin in the flat's narrow corridor, because the sound was good there, and his flatmate Soo-ah stopped whatever she was doing to listen. 'You look different when you play,' she told him one night. 'Different how?' 'Awake.' Marek laughed it off, but he knew what she meant. His code assignments got done, correctly and on time, like chores. The violin got his real attention, the kind where he forgot to eat. Both mattered. He just noticed that one of them had to be pushed, and the other pulled him.

qa.q: When did Marek's lectures start?
qa.a: They started at eight.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's word 'Awake' suggest about Marek's inner state?
qa.a: It suggests Marek feels alive and absorbed with the violin, while he feels dutiful but flat about coding, even though he truly wants the security.

qa.q: How could Marek bring more energy to his course?
qa.a: He could look for areas that connect both motives, such as audio software, so the course pulls him instead of only being pushed.

qa.a: Soo-ah stops whatever she is doing to listen, and sees a side of him that his coursework never shows.

At 11 p.m., the engineering hostel's common room was empty except for Hansa and an old harmonium someone had left behind.
Her roommate Indu found her there. “Thermodynamics quiz tomorrow, Hansa.”
“I know. I've done it. Mostly.” Hansa's fingers kept moving over the keys, soft, so the warden wouldn't hear.
“You never play like this in the lab,” Indu said.
Hansa laughed. “The lab pays the rent later. This…” She stopped. “Papa says engineers never go hungry. He's right. I want that too. A steady salary, a flat for Amma.”
“And this?”
“This is the only hour of my day I don't check the clock.”
Indu sat down. “Both can be true, you know.”
Hansa nodded slowly. She did her circuits homework on time but with half her heart. The harmonium got the other half.

qa.q: What instrument did Hansa play in the common room?
qa.a: She played an old harmonium someone had left behind.

qa.q: How does Hansa feel about her two sets of reasons?
qa.a: She feels torn: she truly wants the security of an engineering salary for Amma, but only feels fully alive and free when she plays music.

qa.q: What could help Hansa bring more energy to both parts of her life?

qa.a: Indu sees that both motives are real and doesn't tell her to choose one, which may help Hansa feel less guilty.

passage:
Subject: Still playing (sort of)

Arohi Didi,

You asked how second year is going. Honestly? Two answers.

The first: I'm doing okay in civil engineering. I chose it because Papa's shop barely survived Covid, and I wanted a job nobody can take away. That reason is real. I still believe it.

The second: I miss the sitar more than I expected. I practise at 6 a.m., before labs, because that's the only time I feel like myself. On weekdays I drag myself to surveying; on Sundays I play for four hours without noticing.

I think that's why my grades are fine but not great. Part of me shows up to class, and part of me stays with the sitar.

I don't know how to fix it yet. Maybe I don't have to choose. Maybe I just need to stop pretending I only have one reason.

Nilesh

I'm Vikas. I picked mechanical engineering because my uncle said it's safe. Placements, a good salary, maybe a job abroad. And I want that. I watched my parents count every rupee. That's not nothing.

First week of July. Irfan filled in the form for mechanical engineering. "Good jobs, good salary," he told his roommate Ujjwal. "Abbu will stop worrying." In his cupboard, under his shirts, was the old guitar he'd played since Class 8.
Five weeks later. Irfan sat through thermodynamics half asleep. He'd been up till two, playing guitar on the hostel roof. In the lab, he did the minimum. Ujjwal asked, "Do you even like engineering?" "I like what it'll give me," Irfan said. "Security. That matters." "And the guitar?" "That's just for me."
Three months later. Irfan joined the college band, two evenings a week. On other days he studied properly, even stayed back for a machine design doubt. "Engineering pays the rent," he said. "Music keeps me awake enough to do it." Both reasons were true, and he'd stopped pretending either one wasn't.

qa.q: Until what time was Irfan up playing guitar?
qa.a: He'd been up till two, playing guitar on the hostel roof.

qa.q: Why did Irfan choose engineering while loving music, and how did that feel at first?
qa.a: He wanted security and to ease Abbu's worry, but the pull toward music left him drained and half asleep, doing only the minimum.

qa.q: What helped Irfan bring more energy to both sides?
qa.a: Joining the college band two evenings a week and admitting both motives were real, which let him study properly on other days.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see Irfan's change over the three months?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably noticed Irfan seeming more awake and settled once he stopped hiding his love for music.

grounding: Over three months a student who chose engineering for security while drawn to music admits both motives are real, and the tension shapes his energy.

passage: Yusuf, you want to know why I became a nurse when I loved singing? Let your Hansa Nani tell you. I was nineteen. My father had just lost his job at the mill. Nursing meant a stipend, a hostel, a job waiting at the end. Singing meant nothing but hope. So I chose nursing, and I told everyone it was my calling. But in the first year I was so tired and flat. I did my duties, but my heart wasn't in the ward. At night, in the hostel bathroom, I sang old songs to the tiles. One day the matron heard me and asked me to sing for the patients at the Christmas gathering. I sang, and an old man in bed six cried and held my hand. After that, something changed. The nursing was for the family, and the singing was for me, and both belonged in that ward.

passage: The rain had flooded the road to the college, the electronics exam was at ten, and the tabla audition for the city youth festival was at four the same afternoon. Tanvir had chosen engineering for one reason he never hid: good jobs. His father drove an auto, and the family needed a steady salary. But tabla was the thing he thought about in every lecture. He waded through the water to the exam hall, wrote the paper quickly and well, then caught a crowded bus across town, his tabla wrapped in plastic. Parveen, who played sitar, met him at the gate. "You look half-dead." "Engineering in the morning, music in the evening," he grinned. "I need both." "Which one do you love?" He thought about it. "The music. But the engineering lets me keep it. Both are real." He played that afternoon with wet shoes, and better than he'd played all year.

passage:
Christmas week in Bengaluru, and the hostel was half empty. Elizabeth sat on her bed with the thermodynamics textbook open at the same page for forty minutes, while down the corridor someone played carols on a cheap keyboard, badly.
She knew exactly why she had chosen engineering. Her father had said it on the phone again that morning: steady jobs, good salary, no begging for gigs. And she agreed with him. She did. She wanted a flat of her own one day and never to worry about rent.
But when Vaibhav knocked and said, "The guy next door is murdering 'Silent Night', come fix it," she was off the bed before he finished. For two hours she sat at the keyboard, rearranging chords and teaching Vaibhav a harmony, never once checking the time.
Back in her room, the textbook was still on page 212. She sighed and started reading.

qa.q: Which page was the textbook still open at?
qa.a: Page 212.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth feel about her choice of engineering?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels torn: she truly wants the security her father describes, yet music pulls her so strongly that she loses track of time, while the textbook feels like a weight.

qa.q: What could help Elizabeth handle both sets of reasons?
qa.a: She could admit both motives are real, keep music in her week on purpose, and talk honestly with her father or a mentor about the balance she wants.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Elizabeth at the keyboard?
qa.a: Vaibhav sees someone lit up and fully absorbed, arranging chords for two hours, which may say more about what she loves than anything she says. 🎶

grounding: A student chose engineering for security while music pulls at her, and the tension shows in how much energy she brings to each.
